Lecture 17

Sure and almost sure convergence, the SLLN and the sample mean

Deck B, slides 11 to 19 · 38 min read · 11 practice problems

Solutions stay collapsed until you click them.

Where we are. L16 left us with a question: what does "Xn​→X" even mean when every Xn​ is random? We already know what convergence means for numbers and for functions. The good news is that we can just reuse that, because of one fact from L1:

A random variable is just a function X:Ω→R. All the randomness is in which ω gets picked.

So once ω is fixed, X1​(ω),X2​(ω),X3​(ω),… is a plain old sequence of numbers, and we can ask if it converges. We'll call this sequence the path of ω.

This lecture gives two ways of using that idea:

  • Sure convergence: the path converges to X(ω) for every ω.
  • Almost sure convergence: the path converges for every ω except a set of ω's with probability 0.

After that we get:

  1. the strong law of large numbers (SLLN), the big example of almost sure convergence, which is also why Monte Carlo (L15) works;
  2. the Borel–Cantelli criterion, the main tool for proving almost sure convergence;
  3. a warning: almost sure convergence does not make E[Xn​] converge.

Part A: the slides

Slide 11/30: Recap

On the slide. Convergence of Xn​→X. X could even be a deterministic number. The Xn​'s could be dependent on each other. Each Xn​ could have a different law (pmf/pdf).

Same as the last slide of L16 (examples there). The point of the three bullets is that the setting is very general:

  • The limit can be a constant. In fact it usually is: in the SLLN the limit is the number μ. A constant c is still a random variable, it's just the function that equals c for every ω.
  • The Xn​ can depend on each other, and usually do. For example μ^​n​ and μ^​n+1​ share n data points. So don't assume independence unless a theorem says so.
  • Each Xn​ can have its own distribution, like Xn​∼N(0,n1​), which gets narrower as n grows.

What can't change: all the Xn​ and X live on the same Ω. Otherwise comparing Xn​(ω) with X(ω) makes no sense. (Convergence in distribution in L18 is the one mode that drops this.)

Slide 12/30: Pointwise or sure convergence

On the slide. {Xn​,n≥0} converges to X pointwise or surely if for all ω∈Ω we have limn→∞​Xn​(ω)=X(ω). Example: Ω={H,T},

Xn​={n1​1+n1​​if ω=Hif ω=T​andX={01​if ω=Hif ω=T.​

This is just pointwise convergence of functions (L16 slide 8), where the functions happen to be Xn​:Ω→R. Fix ω, look at its path, check it goes to X(ω). Do that for every ω.

In ϵ–N form:

for every ω∈Ω and every ϵ>0, ∃N(ϵ,ω) such that ∣Xn​(ω)−X(ω)∣<ϵ for all n>N(ϵ,ω).

N is allowed to depend on ω, same as pointwise convergence of functions.

Notice that P doesn't show up anywhere in this definition. It's purely about functions. That's why it's called "sure": whatever outcome you get, the path converges.

The example. One toss decides everything, and there are only two outcomes, so just check both.

  • ω=H: the path is 1,21​,31​,⋯→0=X(H). ✓
  • ω=T: the path is 2,23​,34​,⋯→1=X(T). ✓

Both paths converge to the right value, so Xn​→X surely.

It's actually even uniform: ∣Xn​(ω)−X(ω)∣=n1​ for both outcomes, so N=ϵ1​ works for every ω (L16 slide 9).

Also notice Xn​=X+n1​. The toss happens once, and after that the path just slides towards X. It doesn't matter at all whether the coin is fair. Another way to see that sure convergence doesn't care about probabilities.

Slide 13/30: Almost sure convergence

On the slide. Xn​ converges to X almost surely if P(ω∈Ω:limn→∞​Xn​(ω)=X(ω))=1. The set of outcomes where convergence does not happen has measure 0: P{ω∈Ω:limn​Xn​(ω)=X(ω)}=0. Example: Ω=[0,1], pick a number uniformly in [0,1]. Let Xn​(ω)=ωn and X(ω)=0 for all ω. Xn​(ω)→X(ω) for ω∈[0,1). Xn​(ω)→X(ω) for ω=1, and P{ω=1} [=0]. This is almost sure convergence as P{[0,1)}=1.

(The slide is missing "=0" after P{ω=1}.)

Sure convergence is too strict. One weird ω that basically never happens can break it. Almost sure convergence fixes this: some paths are allowed to misbehave, as long as all of them together have probability 0.

Put all the "good" ω's (the ones whose path converges to the right thing) into one set:

C={ω:Xn​(ω)→X(ω)}.

Then

Xn​a.s.​X⟺P(C)=1⟺P(Cc)=0​

Bad ω's can exist, they just have no probability. You'll also see this written as "with probability 1" (w.p.1) or just "a.s.".

The example. It's xn from L16 slide 8, except now ω is picked uniformly from [0,1] and Xn​(ω)=ωn.

  • ω∈[0,1): ωn→0, since a number below 1 keeps shrinking when you multiply it by itself (e.g. 0.9,0.81,0.729,…). Good.
  • ω=1: 1n=1 forever, never gets to 0. Bad.
  • So C=[0,1), and since a single point has probability 0 under the uniform, P(C)=1−0=1.

So Xn​a.s.​0, but not surely, because of ω=1.

Sure vs almost sure. Sure ⇒ almost sure (if every ω is good, C=Ω and P(Ω)=1). The converse is false (the example above).

In probability we basically always use almost sure. If you change a random variable on a probability-0 set, no probability, expectation or distribution changes. So caring about those sets would mean caring about something you can't even detect. That's why sure convergence pretty much disappears after this slide.

Another way to write it (we need this on slide 18). For a single ω, "the path converges" means: for every ϵ>0, the path is within ϵ of X(ω) from some point on. So

Xn​a.s.​X⟺with probability 1, for every ϵ>0, ∣Xn​−X∣<ϵ for all large enough n.

Now flip it and look at the bad events En​(ϵ)={∣Xn​−X∣≥ϵ}. "Within ϵ for all large n" is the same as "only finitely many En​(ϵ) happen". So:

Xn​a.s.​X⟺for each ϵ>0,P(En​(ϵ) happens for infinitely many n)=0.

(Why can "for every ϵ" move outside the P? It's enough to check ϵ=1,21​,31​,…, which is countably many, and a countable union of probability-0 sets still has probability 0. Slide 18 uses exactly this trick.)

So a.s. convergence is about the entire tail of the path: the ϵ-sized mistakes have to stop for good. Remember this, because convergence in probability in L18 only asks that mistakes get rare at each fixed n, which is weaker.

Slide 14/30: Example 2, the strong law of large numbers

On the slide. Let {Xn​,n≥0} be a sequence of i.i.d. random variables with mean μ and Sn​=∑i=1n​Xi​. Then nSn​​→μ a.s. Toss a biased coin (probability of heads μ) repeatedly. What is ω and Ω? Let Xi​ be the outcome of the i-th toss and Sn​ the number of heads in n tosses. The empirical mean is nSn​​.

X1​,X2​,… i.i.d., E∣X1​∣<∞, μ=E[X1​]⟹μ^​n​=nSn​​a.s.​μ​

So: keep averaging i.i.d. copies and the running average settles at the true mean, on basically every path.

The exact condition is that the mean is finite, E∣X1​∣<∞. You don't need a finite variance. (The short proof in B12 assumes more than that, but only to make the proof easier.)

What are ω and Ω? (the blue question). This is the important part of the slide. The SLLN is about nSn​​ as n→∞, so it's a statement about the whole infinite sequence of tosses. That means one outcome has to be the entire infinite sequence, not one toss.

  • One outcome is an infinite sequence of tosses, like ω=(H,T,T,H,H,…).
  • The sample space is all such sequences:
Ω={H,T}N={(ω1​,ω2​,…):ωi​∈{H,T}}.

This is uncountable (same idea as binary expansions of numbers in [0,1]).

  • The random variables just read off the coordinates: Xi​(ω)=1 if ωi​=H, else 0. So Sn​(ω) = number of H's in the first n spots, and nSn​(ω)​ = fraction of heads so far.

With this, the SLLN says exactly

P({ω:nSn​(ω)​→μ})=1,

which is slide 13's definition with nSn​​ in place of Xn​ and the constant μ in place of X.

Bad ω's do exist.

  • ω=(H,H,H,…) gives nSn​​=1 for all n. Bad whenever μ<1.
  • The block sequence from L16 (blocks of H's and T's with doubling lengths) makes nSn​​ swing up and down forever, so no limit at all.

There are actually uncountably many bad sequences. Their total probability is still 0.

Probability 0 isn't the same as impossible. For 0<μ<1, every single sequence has probability 0. The chance that the first n tosses match a fixed pattern is a product of n factors, each at most max(μ,1−μ)<1, so it's at most max(μ,1−μ)n→0. So all-heads isn't "less possible" than any other particular sequence. What the SLLN says is that the set of sequences with the wrong fraction of heads is negligible.

Why we care in this course.

  • Monte Carlo (L15 slide 17). g(U1​),g(U2​),… are i.i.d. with finite mean θ=∫01​g, so their average goes to θ with probability 1. That's literally why Monte Carlo works.
  • Probability = long-run frequency. Take Xi​=1{A happens on trial i}. Then E[Xi​]=P(A), so the fraction of trials where A happens goes to P(A) almost surely. The "frequency" idea of probability is now a theorem.
  • The sample mean as an estimator (slide 15).

When it breaks. No finite mean, no SLLN (in general). For i.i.d. standard Cauchy, nSn​​ is again standard Cauchy for every n (a known Cauchy property). Averaging doesn't shrink the spread at all, so the running mean never settles. This is the simulation from L15 Part B, B10.

Slide 15/30: Detour, the sample mean as an estimator

On the slide. Now that we know nSn​​→μ, we can use μ^​n​:=nSn​​ as an "estimator" for the mean, especially when the underlying distribution is not known. The estimator μ^​n​ is a random variable. What is its CDF? What are its mean and variance? μ^​n​ is an "unbiased estimator" since E[μ^​n​]=μ. Var(μ^​n​)=nσ2​. We will soon see the CLT, which will tell us the CDF of μ^​n​ without any information on the law of the Xi​.

Say we don't know the distribution and want μ. The SLLN basically tells us what to do: average the data. An estimator is just a formula that turns data into a guess. (L21 does estimators properly.)

The key thing: μ^​n​ is itself random. One data set gives one value μ^​n​(ω), a different data set gives a different value. So it has a mean, a variance and a distribution, and those tell us how good the estimator is.

Mean. Linearity of expectation, no independence needed:

E[μ^​n​]=E[n1​i=1∑n​Xi​]=n1​i=1∑n​E[Xi​]=n1​⋅nμ=μ.

When the expected value of an estimator equals the thing it estimates, we call it unbiased. It can be off for a given data set, but on average it's right, it doesn't lean too high or too low.

Variance. Pull out n1​ (it comes out squared, since Var(aY)=a2Var(Y)), then use that variances of independent variables add (toolkit fact 5):

Var(μ^​n​)=n21​Var(i=1∑n​Xi​)=n21​⋅nσ2=nσ2​.

This step does need independence (or at least uncorrelated Xi​). Otherwise covariance terms show up.

E[μ^​n​]=μ,Var(μ^​n​)=nσ2​,SD(μ^​n​)=n​σ​​

So the estimator is centred at μ and its spread, the standard error n​σ​, shrinks with n. Because of the square root it shrinks slowly: halving the error needs 4× the data, and one more correct decimal place needs 100×.

For example, Bernoulli(μ) data has σ2=μ(1−μ)≤41​, so with n=104 we get SD(μ^​n​)≤1001/2​=0.005.

What's the CDF? Exactly, it depends on the distribution of Xi​, and we only know it in special cases. These come from L14's MGF results, since Sn​=nμ^​n​ is a sum of i.i.d. variables:

Xi​ distribution of Sn​=nμ^​n​ (from)
Bernoulli(p) Binomial(n,p) L14 slide 6
Poisson(λ) Poisson(nλ) L14 slide 5
Exp(λ) Gamma(n,λ) L14 slide 6
N(μ,σ2) N(nμ,nσ2) L14 slide 5

In general there's no closed form. The CLT (L18) gives an approximate answer that works for any distribution, which is what the slide is hinting at:

μ^​n​≈N(μ,nσ2​)for large n.

Same mean and variance as we just computed.

Slide 16/30: Detour, the incremental formula for the sample mean

On the slide. Given μ^​n​, suppose you see an additional sample Xn+1​. How will you compute μ^​n+1​? Naive way: μ^​n+1​=n+1∑i=1n+1​Xi​​. There is an incremental formula that uses μ^​n​:

μ^​n+1​=μ^​n​+n+11​[Xn+1​−μ^​n​].

Such averaging formulas are used extensively in reinforcement learning.

The question: data comes in one point at a time, and you want the updated average after each one. Do you really have to re-add everything every time?

No, because the old mean already "contains" the old sum: Sn​=nμ^​n​. So

  1. Sn+1​=Sn​+Xn+1​=nμ^​n​+Xn+1​,
  2. divide by n+1, and write nμ^​n​=(n+1)μ^​n​−μ^​n​ so a full μ^​n​ splits off:
μ^​n+1​=n+1nμ^​n​+Xn+1​​=n+1(n+1)μ^​n​−μ^​n​+Xn+1​​=μ^​n​+n+11​(Xn+1​−μ^​n​).
μ^​n+1​=μ^​n​+n+11​(Xn+1​−μ^​n​)​

How to read it: new estimate = old estimate + (step size) × (new point − old estimate).

  • Xn+1​−μ^​n​ is how far the new point is from what we currently think the mean is.
  • We move n+11​ of the way towards the new point. New point above the mean, mean goes up, and vice versa.
  • The steps get smaller as n grows (one more point barely changes an average of a million points), so the estimate settles down, which matches the SLLN.

Why bother? The naive way stores all the data and does O(n) work per update. The incremental way stores just μ^​n​ and n, and does O(1) work.

The RL remark on the slide: RL updates look like Q←Q+α(target−Q). With α=n+11​ that's exactly our running mean. With a fixed α, each old point's weight gets multiplied by 1−α every step, so you get an exponentially weighted average that slowly forgets old data.

Quick check. Data 4,8,6,10:

  • μ^​1​=4
  • μ^​2​=4+21​(8−4)=6
  • μ^​3​=6+31​(6−6)=6 (new point equals the mean, so nothing changes)
  • μ^​4​=6+41​(10−6)=7

And 44+8+6+10​=7. ✓

Slide 17/30: Recap, modes of convergence

On the slide. Sure convergence (box). Almost sure convergence (box). SLLN: {Xn​} i.i.d. with mean μ and Sn​=∑Xi​; then μ^​n​:=nSn​​→μ a.s. The estimator μ^​n​ has mean μ and variance nσ2​. μ^​n+1​=μ^​n​+n+11​[Xn+1​−μ^​n​].

Nothing new. So far:

  • Sure: every path converges. Almost sure: the paths that don't converge have probability 0. Sure ⇒ a.s., not the other way.
  • SLLN is an a.s. statement about the sample mean.
  • Sample mean: unbiased, variance nσ2​, and can be updated in O(1).

Slide 18/30: The Borel–Cantelli lemma

On the slide. Self-study: Theorem 7.5 (probabilitycourse.com). Consider a sequence of random variables X1​,X2​,…. If for all ϵ we have ∑n=1∞​P(∣Xn​−X∣>ϵ)<∞, then Xn​→X a.s. This is only a sufficient condition for almost sure convergence! Thm 7.6 (HW) gives necessary and sufficient conditions. Lots of problems in probabilitycourse; practice them!

Proving a.s. convergence straight from the definition means finding the set C and computing P(C). That's fine when Ω=[0,1] and everything is explicit (slide 13), but most of the time you can't do it. Theorem 7.5 lets you work with something much easier: P(∣Xn​−X∣>ϵ) at each single n.

n=1∑∞​P(∣Xn​−X∣>ϵ)<∞  for every ϵ>0⟹Xn​a.s.​X​

So if the chance of being off by more than ϵ shrinks fast enough that the sum is finite (like n21​, n1.011​, e−n, but not n1​), for every ϵ, then you get a.s. convergence.

Why you'd expect this: ∑n​P(En​)=E[∑n​1En​​] is the expected number of bad events. If that's finite, the actual number of bad events is finite with probability 1. Finitely many mistakes means after the last one, the path stays within ϵ forever.

Proof (the self-study part). Fix ϵ, and let En​={∣Xn​−X∣>ϵ}.

  1. The tail is small. For any m, by the union bound (toolkit fact 8),
P(n≥m⋃​En​)≤n≥m∑​P(En​),

and the right side is the tail of a convergent series, so it goes to 0 as m→∞. 2. Infinitely many En​ has probability 0. If infinitely many En​ happen, then for any m at least one En​ with n≥m happens. So "En​ infinitely often" sits inside ⋃n≥m​En​ for every m:

P(En​ infinitely often)≤P(n≥m⋃​En​)for every m.

Let m→∞, the right side goes to 0 by step 1, so the left side is 0. This step by itself is the (first) Borel–Cantelli lemma:

n∑​P(En​)<∞⟹P(En​ infinitely often)=0​

i.e. with probability 1, only finitely many En​ happen. 3. All ϵ at once. Step 2 gives: with probability 1, ∣Xn​−X∣≤ϵ for all large n. Do this for ϵ=1,21​,31​,…. Each one has a probability-0 exception, and countably many probability-0 sets together still have probability 0. So with probability 1 it works for every ϵ=k1​ at the same time. Any ϵ>0 is bigger than some k1​, so that's exactly Xn​(ω)→X(ω). □

Note that independence was never used. Theorem 7.5 works no matter how the Xn​ depend on each other. (Compare the second Borel–Cantelli lemma below, which does need it.)

It's only sufficient. In slide 19's example, ∑n​P(∣Xn​∣>ϵ)=∑n1​=∞, but Xn​→0 a.s. anyway. So if the sum diverges, Theorem 7.5 just tells you nothing.

Theorem 7.6 (the HW): necessary and sufficient. For ϵ>0 let

Am​={∣Xn​−X∣<ϵ for all n≥m},

the event that from time m onwards the path stays within ϵ of X forever. Then

Xn​a.s.​X⟺m→∞lim​P(Am​)=1  for every ϵ>0​

The difference from 7.5: there we looked at one n at a time, here Am​ looks at the whole future after m. That's exactly what a.s. convergence is about (slide 13), which is why this one goes both ways.

Proof.

  • A1​⊆A2​⊆⋯, since staying close from time m on means you also stay close from m+1 on.
  • ⋃m​Am​ = "from some point on, always within ϵ" = "eventually always within ϵ".
  • Continuity of probability for increasing events (toolkit fact 8):
m→∞lim​P(Am​)=P(m⋃​Am​)=P(eventually always within ϵ).

(⇒) If ω∈C (its path converges), the path is eventually within ϵ. So C⊆⋃m​Am​, and P(C)=1 forces the limit to be 1.

(⇐) If the limit is 1 for each ϵ=k1​, each event "eventually within k1​" has probability 1. Intersect these countably many probability-1 events, still probability 1. On the intersection the path is eventually within k1​ for every k, i.e. it converges. □

Using 7.6 in practice. Compute or bound P(Am​). This is really easy when the path gets stuck once it reaches the limit (once it's 0 it stays 0): then Am​ is just one event at time m. See slide 19 and B5.

The second Borel–Cantelli lemma.

En​ independent and n∑​P(En​)=∞⟹P(En​ infinitely often)=1​

If the events are independent and the expected number of them is infinite, then infinitely many actually happen. This is what you use to show a sequence does not converge a.s. Independence really matters here, slide 19 shows the conclusion can fail without it. It comes up on slide 20 (L18) and in Part B.

Slide 19/30: Another example of a.s. convergence

On the slide. Consider a uniform random variable U and define Xn​=n1{U≤n1​}​: Xn​=n when U≤n1​ and Xn​=0 otherwise. Given a realization of U, what can you say about the sequence {Xn​}? Once an Xn​ is zero, all higher-indexed variables are also zero! This happens for all realizations other than U=0. In that case, since 0≤n1​ for all n, the Xn​'s run off to infinity and we don't see convergence to 0. But P(U=0)=0. Does E[Xn​]→0? Almost sure convergence does not imply that the means converge!

The important thing here: there's only one U, drawn once, and every Xn​ is a function of it. So the Xn​ are very dependent, and the outcome is basically just ω=U.

Fix U=u and follow the path.

  • u>0: u≤n1​ means n≤u1​. So Xn​=n while n≤u1​, and Xn​=0 after that. The thresholds n1​ only go down, so once n1​<u it stays that way, and once Xn​=0 it stays 0.
  • u=0: 0≤n1​ always, so Xn​=n forever and the path blows up.
u path X1​,X2​,X3​,…
0.6 1,0,0,0,…
0.3 1,2,3,0,0,…
0.01 1,2,…,100,0,0,…
0 1,2,3,4,⋯→∞

The only bad outcome is u=0, and P(U=0)=0, so Xn​a.s.​0. (Not surely though, because of u=0.)

The means. Xn​ is either n or 0, so

E[Xn​]=n⋅P(U≤n1​)+0=n⋅n1​=1for every n,

which gives

E[Xn​]=1→0=E[nlim​Xn​].

Why don't the means follow? Each Xn​ is 0 with probability 1−n1​, but it's the huge value n with the tiny probability n1​. Huge × tiny is exactly 1, so the mean stays at 1. People call this mass escaping to infinity.

A.s. convergence can't see this because it looks at one ω at a time. For a fixed u>0 the big values stop after u1​ steps. But at any time n, the ω's that still have a big value (those with u≤n1​) have such a big value that they hold the average up. Convergence in mean (L18) is the mode that catches this, and it fails here: E∣Xn​−0∣=1→0.

Link with slide 18.

  • 7.5 is no use: for 0<ϵ<1, P(∣Xn​∣>ϵ)=P(U≤n1​)=n1​, and ∑n1​=∞. Yet Xn​→0 a.s. This is the example showing 7.5 is only sufficient.
  • 7.6 works: since the path gets stuck at 0, being 0 from time m on is the same as being 0 at time m:
Am​={Xn​=0 for all n≥m}={U>m1​},P(Am​)=1−m1​→1. ✓
  • Second Borel–Cantelli doesn't apply: the events {U≤n1​} have a divergent sum, but they're nested, not independent. That's exactly why infinitely many of them don't happen.

Next slide (start of L18) uses the same formula with independent Un​, one fresh uniform per n, and things change completely.

Part B: extra worked examples and problems

General plan for "does Xn​→X a.s.?" Pretty much every problem here is one of these:

  1. If Ω is simple (one coin toss, one uniform on [0,1]), just fix ω, work out the path, and find where it fails. Is that set probability 0?
  2. Compute P(∣Xn​−X∣>ϵ) and check if the sum is finite. If yes, Theorem 7.5 finishes it (no independence needed). If the sum diverges, this tells you nothing.
  3. Compute P(Am​) for Theorem 7.6. Easy when the path gets stuck at its limit.
  4. To show it fails: find a positive-probability set where the path doesn't converge, or use second Borel–Cantelli (needs independence).

For limits of averages: SLLN, plus the fact that continuous functions of a.s. limits are a.s. limits (B9).

B1 (probabilitycourse 7.2.7, Example 1). A fair coin is tossed once. Xn​=n+1n​ if H, and Xn​=(−1)n if T. Does Xn​ converge almost surely?

Solution

Solution. Only two outcomes, so look at both paths.

  • H: 21​,32​,43​,⋯→1. Converges.
  • T: −1,1,−1,1,… keeps flipping, no limit.

So the path converges only on {H}, and P(limXn​=1)=P(H)=21​. We'd need this to be 1. It's 21​, so Xn​ does not converge a.s. (to 1 or to anything else).

The bad set is fine only if it has probability 0. Here it has probability 21​.

B2 (probabilitycourse 7.2.7, Example 2). Ω=[0,1] with the uniform probability. Xn​(s)=1 if 0≤s<2nn+1​ and 0 otherwise; X(s)=1 if 0≤s<21​ and 0 otherwise. Show Xn​a.s.​X.

Solution

Solution. First rewrite the cutoff:

2nn+1​=21​+2n1​,

which decreases down to 21​. So Xn​ is the indicator of [0,21​+2n1​), an interval shrinking to [0,21​]. Now three cases for s:

  • s<21​: s is below every cutoff, so Xn​(s)=1=X(s) for all n. ✓
  • s>21​: once the cutoff drops to s or below, i.e. 21​+2n1​≤s, i.e. n≥2s−11​, we get Xn​(s)=0=X(s), and it stays 0. ✓
  • s=21​: 21​<21​+2n1​ always, so Xn​(21​)=1 for all n, but X(21​)=0. ✗

The bad set is just {21​}, which has probability 0. So Xn​→X a.s. (but not surely).

The whole issue is the endpoint: the intervals shrink to [0,21​], but X uses [0,21​). "Almost" lets us ignore that one point.

B3 (probabilitycourse 7.2.7, Example 3). Xn​=±n1​ with probability 21​ each. Show Xn​a.s.​0.

Solution

Solution. Whatever the sign is, ∣Xn​∣=n1​. So for fixed ϵ>0,

P(∣Xn​∣>ϵ)=P(n1​>ϵ)={10​n<ϵ1​n≥ϵ1​.​

So ∑n​P(∣Xn​∣>ϵ) has at most ⌊ϵ1​⌋ nonzero terms, so it's finite, and Theorem 7.5 gives Xn​a.s.​0.

Actually it's even sure convergence: ∣Xn​(ω)∣≤n1​ for every ω, whatever the signs are and however they depend on each other. The size isn't random at all, only the sign is.

B4 (probabilitycourse 7.2.7, Example 4; last year's HW8 Q1(b)). Xn​ independent, Xn​∼ Bernoulli(n1​). Does Xn​→0 almost surely?

Solution

Solution. No. First, 7.5 doesn't help: for 0<ϵ<1, P(∣Xn​∣>ϵ)=P(Xn​=1)=n1​, and ∑n1​=∞.

So use 7.6. Since Xn​∈{0,1}, being within ϵ<1 of 0 just means being 0:

Am​={Xn​=0 for all n≥m}.

We can't directly handle "for all n≥m", so bound it by a finite piece. For any N≥m, Am​⊆{Xm​=⋯=XN​=0}, and by independence that's a product:

P(Am​)≤P(Xm​=0,…,XN​=0)=(1−m1​)⋯(1−N1​)=mm−1​⋅m+1m​⋯NN−1​=Nm−1​.

(It telescopes: each numerator cancels the denominator before it.) This works for every N≥m, and Nm−1​→0 as N→∞. So P(Am​)=0 for every m, and

m→∞lim​P(Am​)=0=1.

By 7.6, no a.s. convergence. In fact, with probability 1 there are infinitely many 1s: no matter how far out you go, another 1 shows up.

Shortcut: the events {Xn​=1} are independent with ∑n1​=∞, so second Borel–Cantelli says infinitely many happen, with probability 1. Done in one line.

Compare with slide 19. In both, P(Xn​=0)=n1​, so each Xn​ has the same distribution! The only difference is how they depend on each other. On slide 19 the events {U≤n1​} are nested (all from one U), so the nonzero values stop. Here they're independent, so they keep coming back. A.s. convergence depends on the joint behaviour, not just each Xn​ separately.

B5 (last year's HW8 Q10 and HW7 Q4). Yn​∼ Bernoulli(n+1n​) independent, and Xn+1​=Y1​Y2​⋯Yn​. Show Xn​a.s.​0 (and hence in probability).

Solution

Solution. A product of 0s and 1s is 1 only if every factor is 1. By independence,

P(Xn+1​=1)=k=1∏n​P(Yk​=1)=k=1∏n​k+1k​=21​⋅32​⋯n+1n​=n+11​→0,

telescoping again. So P(Xn​=1)=n1​.

Each step multiplies by Yn​∈{0,1}, so the path can only stay the same or drop to 0, and once it's 0 it's 0 forever. Paths look like 1,1,…,1,0,0,0,…

So the path gets stuck at 0, and being 0 from time m on is the same as being 0 at time m:

Am​={Xn​=0 for all n≥m}={Xm​=0},P(Am​)=1−m1​→1.

By 7.6, Xn​→0 a.s.

Another way to see it: the only way to never converge is Yk​=1 for every k. That event is inside {Xn+1​=1} for every n, so its probability is at most n+11​ for all n, i.e. 0.

Again ∑n​P(Xn​=1)=∑n1​=∞, so 7.5 can't do it. This one is like slide 19, not B4: the events {Xn​=1} are nested (each one implies all the earlier ones). Nested events can have a divergent sum and still give a.s. convergence.

B6 (probabilitycourse 7.2.8, Problem 2). X1​,X2​,… i.i.d. U(0,1) and Yn​=min(X1​,…,Xn​). Show Yn​a.s.​0.

Solution

Solution. The min is above ϵ exactly when all the Xi​ are above ϵ (the usual min trick from L13). For 0<ϵ<1, by independence,

P(Yn​>ϵ)=P(X1​>ϵ,…,Xn​>ϵ)=(1−ϵ)n.

That's geometric with ratio 1−ϵ<1:

n=1∑∞​(1−ϵ)n=ϵ1−ϵ​<∞.

So 7.5 gives Yn​→0 a.s. (For ϵ≥1 the probabilities are all 0 anyway.)

Geometric decay is always summable, so that's an easy win. You could also use 7.6 here since Yn​ only goes down: once below ϵ it stays below, so Am​={Ym​<ϵ} and P(Am​)=1−(1−ϵ)m→1.

B7 (probabilitycourse 7.2.8, Problem 3). Xn​∼N(0,n1​). Show Xn​a.s.​0.

Solution

Solution. Standardize: Xn​ has the same distribution as n​Z​ with Z∼N(0,1). So

P(∣Xn​∣>ϵ)=P(∣Z∣>ϵn​)=2(1−Φ(ϵn​)).

We can't sum Φ's exactly, so bound them with the Gaussian tail bound 1−Φ(x)≤21​e−x2/2 for x≥0. With x=ϵn​, x2=ϵ2n:

n∑​P(∣Xn​∣>ϵ)≤n∑​2⋅21​e−ϵ2n/2=n∑​(e−ϵ2/2)n<∞,

geometric with ratio e−ϵ2/2<1. So 7.5 gives a.s. convergence.

The question never says how the Xn​ depend on each other, and we didn't need it, since 7.5 doesn't use independence. Also, Chebyshev only gives P(∣Xn​∣>ϵ)≤nϵ21​, and that sum diverges, so you really do need the Gaussian tail here.

B8 (probabilitycourse 7.2.8, Problem 4). On Ω=[0,1] with uniform probability, Xn​(s)=n+1n​s+(1−s)n and X(s)=s. Show Xn​a.s.​X.

Solution

Solution. Fix s and handle the two terms separately.

  • n+1n​→1, so n+1n​s→s for every s.
  • (1−s)n: if 0<s≤1 then 0≤1−s<1, so (1−s)n→0 (same as slide 13). If s=0 it's 1n=1 forever.

So for 0<s≤1, Xn​(s)→s+0=s=X(s). ✓ At s=0, Xn​(0)=0+1=1 for all n, so it goes to 1=0=X(0). ✗

The bad set is {0}, probability 0, so Xn​a.s.​X.

B9 (Bertsekas Problem 13; last year's Tutorial 8 Q7). (a) If Xn​→a and Yn​→b almost surely, show Xn​+Yn​→a+b almost surely. (b) Find limn→∞​∑i=1n​Xi​∑i=1n​Xi2​​ for i.i.d. Xi​∼U[0,1].

Solution

Solution. (a) Idea: throw out the bad ω's of both sequences together. What's left still has probability 1, and on it everything is just normal real analysis.

  • Let A={Xn​→a} and B={Yn​→b}. Both have probability 0.
  • For ω∈/A∪B, Xn​(ω)→a and Yn​(ω)→b are ordinary convergent sequences, so the sum goes to a+b.
  • So Xn​+Yn​ can only fail on A∪B, and P(A∪B)≤P(A)+P(B)=0.

Same argument works for products, ratios (if b=0), and any continuous g: g(Xn​,Yn​)→g(a,b) a.s.

(b) Trick: a ratio of sums is a ratio of averages, because the n1​'s cancel:

∑i=1n​Xi​∑i=1n​Xi2​​=n1​∑i=1n​Xi​n1​∑i=1n​Xi2​​.

Now SLLN on top and bottom:

  • top: the Xi2​ are i.i.d. with mean E[X2]=∫01​x2dx=31​, so n1​∑Xi2​a.s.​31​;
  • bottom: n1​∑Xi​a.s.​E[X]=21​.

g(x,y)=yx​ is continuous at (31​,21​) since 21​=0, so by (a)

∑Xi​∑Xi2​​a.s.​1/21/3​=32​.

B10 (Bertsekas Problem 14). Xi​ i.i.d. and Yi​ i.i.d., with finite means and E[Y]=0. Does Zn​=Y1​+⋯+Yn​X1​+⋯+Xn​​ converge almost surely?

Solution

Solution. Yes, same trick as B9(b). Divide top and bottom by n:

Zn​=(Y1​+⋯+Yn​)/n(X1​+⋯+Xn​)/n​.

SLLN: top →E[X], bottom →E[Y], a.s. Since E[Y]=0 the ratio is continuous there, so by B9(a)

Zn​a.s.​E[Y]E[X]​.

The two sequences don't need to be independent of each other. Each SLLN only uses i.i.d. within its own sequence, and B9(a) just combines two probability-1 events.

B11 (exam-style contrast with slide 19). Let U1​,U2​,… be independent uniforms and Xn​=n21{Un​≤n21​}. Does Xn​→0 almost surely? What is E[Xn​]?

Solution

Solution. For 0<ϵ<1,

P(∣Xn​∣>ϵ)=P(Un​≤n21​)=n21​,n∑​n21​=6π2​<∞.

So 7.5 gives Xn​→0 a.s., even with independent Un​. The bad events are now rare enough that only finitely many happen.

Means: E[Xn​]=n2⋅P(Un​≤n21​)=n2⋅n21​=1 for all n. So once again the means sit at 1 while the limit is 0.

All three cases next to each other:

set-up P(Xn​=0) a.s. to 0? why
one U: n1{U≤n1​} (slide 19) n1​ yes nested events (7.6)
independent Un​: n1{Un​≤n1​} (L18 slide 20) n1​ no independent, ∑n1​=∞ (2nd B–C)
independent Un​: n21{Un​≤n21​} (this one) n21​ yes ∑n21​<∞ (7.5)

In all three, E[Xn​]=1→0.

B12 (Bertsekas Problems 16 and 18, optional): the SLLN with a finite fourth moment. The standard short proof. It assumes more than the theorem needs: E[Xi4​]<∞. Subtract the mean from every Xi​ first, so E[Xi​]=0 and we need to show nSn​​→0.

  1. A criterion (Problem 16). If Yn​≥0 and ∑n​E[Yn​]<∞, then Yn​→0 a.s. Why: the Yn​ are nonnegative, so sum and expectation can be swapped, E[∑n​Yn​]=∑n​E[Yn​]<∞. A random variable with finite mean is finite with probability 1, so ∑n​Yn​<∞ with probability 1. And the terms of a convergent series go to 0.
  2. Fourth moment of the sum. Expand
E[Sn4​]=E[(i∑​Xi​)4]=i,j,k,l∑​E[Xi​Xj​Xk​Xl​].

Which terms survive?

  • If some index shows up exactly once (say i is different from j,k,l), independence gives E[Xi​Xj​Xk​Xl​]=E[Xi​]E[Xj​Xk​Xl​]=0.
  • All four equal: n terms, each E[X4].
  • Two different indices, each twice: 3 ways to pair up the four slots ({1,2}{3,4}, {1,3}{2,4}, {1,4}{2,3}), times n(n−1) ordered choices of i=j. That's 3n(n−1) terms, each E[Xi2​]E[Xj2​]=(E[X2])2≤E[X4].

So E[Sn4​]≤(n+3n(n−1))E[X4]≤3n2E[X4], i.e. E[Sn4​]≤Cn2 with C=3E[X4] (as in Bertsekas). What matters is that it grows like n2, not n4, thanks to all the cancelling. 3. Use the criterion on Yn​=(nSn​​)4≥0:

n∑​E[Yn​]=n∑​n4E[Sn4​]​≤n∑​n4Cn2​=Cn∑​n21​<∞.

So (nSn​​)4→0 a.s., and taking fourth roots, nSn​​→0 a.s. □

Why the fourth power and not the second? With the second moment you get E[(nSn​​)2]=nσ2​, and ∑n1​=∞, so the criterion doesn't apply. That route only gets you the weak law (L18). The fourth power gives the extra n1​ that makes the sum converge.

The general SLLN (finite mean only) needs a harder proof, which is beyond the course.

B13 (concept check). True or false? (a) If Xn​→X surely then Xn​→X almost surely. (b) If ∑n​P(∣Xn​∣>ϵ)=∞ for some ϵ, then Xn​→0 almost surely. (c) If Xn​a.s.​X then E[Xn​]→E[X].

Answers. (a) True. Every path converges, so C=Ω and P(C)=1. (b) False in general. Slide 19 and B5: the sum is ∑n1​=∞, but Xn​→0 a.s. Theorem 7.5 is only sufficient. It becomes true if the events {∣Xn​∣>ϵ} are independent, by second Borel–Cantelli (like B4). (c) False. Slide 19: Xn​→0 a.s. but E[Xn​]=1 for all n. The rare huge values keep the mean up.
